title: Choosing players and first-time sight reading
summary: He gets the players he wants for recordings and prefers they not see the music beforehand for the edge it brings.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: When you get ready to do a recording like you’ve mentioned, do you always get the people you want?

Yes. I try to anyway. You know I was all set to record last March or April, just before the pandemic. I had it all set up and you know there are certain people that I wanted and I called them and, ‘cause I had certain people in mind for certain parts. And so you know I called well ahead of time. Now they could pull the plug at the last minute if they get a better call, you know like a film or something. But generally I get the people I want you know.
Will they have seen the music before they get there?

Never. No. You know you take players well like Pat, Wayne Bergeron, Bill Cunliffe, all those guys, you know, they don’t need to see it in front. And when somebody wants the music in front I get a little suspicious.
Oh that is a quote right there. Most of us don’t live in that world, I can say.

And you know even the best players, they’re going to make mistakes and they say, ah, mistake, no big deal. I mean everybody does. But generally you know I like that insecurity of seeing it for the first time and having that fire and having that edge. There’s an edge there. Clay Jenkins — talk about —
